title: Cervicogenic Headache
case: Case: A 35-year-old office worker has a right-sided headache that starts at the base of the skull after long computer work. Right neck rotation is limited. Flexion-rotation range is clearly lower on the right than on the left, and C1–C2 palpation reproduces the familiar headache. No nausea, no aura, no red flags.
Working diagnosis: cervicogenic headache. Plan: education, C1–C2 self-SNAG, chin tuck, scapular training, workstation changes, reassess in two weeks.

differentials.name: Migraine
differentials.key: Throbbing pain, nausea, light and sound sensitivity, aura, not triggered by neck movement
differentials.next: Medical review; neck care only if mixed picture

differentials.name: Tension-type headache
differentials.key: Band-like pressure, both sides, mild to moderate, no neck movement trigger

differentials.name: Cluster headache
differentials.key: Severe pain around one eye, watering, restlessness

differentials.name: Occipital neuralgia
differentials.key: Sharp shooting pain along the occipital nerve, tender nerve

differentials.name: Temporomandibular disorder
differentials.key: Jaw pain, clicking, pain with chewing

differentials.name: Giant cell arteritis
differentials.key: Age over 50, new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain with chewing, vision change

differentials.name: Subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis
differentials.key: Sudden severe headache or fever with stiff neck

qa: Why compare the flexion-rotation test between sides? The test looks at the specific segment, and a clear side difference helps show a mobility problem. It does not prove the cause.
Why check for migraine features? Migraine can look similar, and treatment and referral differ.
Headache suddenly becomes the worst of the patient's life during an exam. What do you do? Stop immediately and call emergency services. This is a possible bleeding event.
Why avoid upper cervical manipulation in some patients? Because possible vascular warning signs should be excluded first, and the risk-benefit balance is debated.

Pressure on the neck is tender in a healthy volunteer. Why is tenderness alone not diagnostic? Because neck structures are often tender without disease. The reproduction of the familiar headache is more useful.

fields.Purpose: Check mobility of the C1–C2 segment, where most neck rotation occurs when the neck is fully flexed
fields.Therapist position: At the head, supporting the head with both hands
fields.Starting position: Bring the neck into full comfortable flexion so the lower cervical joints are locked
fields.Action: Keeping flexion, passively rotate the head to one side until firm resistance or symptoms appear. Repeat to the other side
fields.Positive: Clearly reduced rotation on one side compared with the other side and with published reference values, often with the familiar headache [Ref – to verify exact values]
fields.Supports: Upper cervical dysfunction, consistent with a cervical source
fields.Limits: A positive result does not prove that the neck is the cause; a negative result lowers the chance but does not exclude it
fields.Errors: Losing full flexion; rotating too fast; not asking about symptoms
fields.Next step: If positive, consider C1–C2 mobilization and exercise

redFlags.Finding: Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion or rash
Neck pain or headache with dizziness, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, facial numbness, balance loss
New headache after age 50, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision change
redFlags.Immediate action: Refer; vision may be at risk

redFlags.Finding: Progressive neurological deficit, personality change, new seizure
Cancer history, weight loss, night sweats

manual.name: C1–C2 self-SNAG or Mulligan SNAG (sustained natural apophyseal glide)
manual.why: Aims to improve rotation without provoking headache [Ref – to verify]
manual.application: Patient sits. A towel or strap held at C2 gives a gentle forward glide while the patient actively rotates the neck
manual.stop: Dizziness, headache increases, any neurological symptoms

manual.name: Upper cervical mobilization (graded)
manual.why: May reduce headache frequency in the short term [Ref – to verify]
manual.finding: Reduced upper cervical mobility with a familiar response
manual.application: Supine, gentle oscillations at C1–C3, low grade

manual.name: Thoracic mobilization
manual.why: Reduces stiffness that adds to neck load

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: gentle upper cervical mobilization or SNAG (as above), combined with exercise. Evidence suggests that manual therapy plus exercise can help, but it is moderate at best and short-term [Ref – to verify]. Avoid high-velocity upper cervical manipulation in a patient with headache and possible vascular features. The risk to benefit balance is debated and the screen should be thorough.
Is it working? Look for improved rotation on the flexion-rotation test, fewer headache days, and less intense headaches.

exercise.Steps: Lying, nod gently as if saying yes, hold
exercise.Progress when: Can hold with no jaw or neck gripping

exercise.Steps: Sitting, draw shoulder blades back and down
Sitting, gentle side-bend and chin tuck
Short work breaks, gentle movement every 30 minutes

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: a mild ache that settles is acceptable. A headache that builds during an exercise, or dizziness, means stop.

modalities.name: Dry needling or myofascial release
modalities.comment: Evidence is limited and mixed [Ref – to verify]. Use only within scope and training

pathway: Any emergency red flag? Yes: emergency action.
Any urgent red flag? Yes: urgent referral, defer treatment.

One-sided headache starting in the neck, triggered by neck movement or posture, with reduced upper cervical rotation (flexion-rotation test) and a familiar-headache response to upper cervical palpation? Yes: working diagnosis is cervicogenic headache.
Features of migraine or tension-type headache dominate? Yes: treat as a mixed or alternative picture and involve the physician if unclear.
Visit 1: screen, examine, explain the likely source and expected course.
Early: reduce triggers, add gentle range, apply selected manual therapy, begin chin tuck.
Middle: add scapular and deep neck flexor endurance, address work posture.
Late: self-management, return to full activity.
